question_bank_answers.debugging: My debugging process starts by making the problem smaller. I try to reproduce it consistently, isolate where the state first goes wrong, inspect logs and inputs, and keep reducing variables until the failure becomes obvious.
question_bank_answers.code_quality: Good code quality means another engineer can understand the intent quickly, change it safely, and trust the behavior in production. Readability, testing, and clear boundaries matter more to me than cleverness.
question_bank_answers.testing: I think about testing as a way to build confidence around the most important paths and failure cases. I care about catching regressions early and making changes easier to trust over time.
question_bank_answers.ambiguity: When a problem is ambiguous, I start by clarifying the goal, writing down the assumptions that matter most, and finding the smallest version worth testing. That keeps me moving without pretending the problem is already fully defined.
question_bank_answers.ownership: Ownership means staying with the problem until it is truly in a better state, not just until my narrow part is done. It includes follow-through, communication, and making handoff easier for the next person.
question_bank_answers.conflict: When there is disagreement, I try to make the real tradeoff visible and keep the conversation anchored in the outcome we want. Most conflict gets easier once the team agrees on what matters most.
question_bank_answers.leadership: Leadership for me has often meant creating clarity, keeping work moving, and helping the group make better decisions under pressure. I have done that through Solar Racing and student leadership roles, as well as in technical project work.
question_bank_answers.learning_speed: I learn quickly by getting my hands on the real problem early. I read just enough to avoid obvious mistakes, build a small version, and let the work show me where I need more depth.
question_bank_answers.deadlines: I manage deadlines by breaking work into smaller checkpoints, identifying the riskiest parts early, and communicating quickly if something changes. That keeps the schedule realistic instead of reactive.
question_bank_answers.failure_lesson: A useful lesson for me has been that speed without enough visibility creates hidden problems. I now put more effort into small checkpoints, clearer notes, and faster feedback before a problem grows.
question_bank_answers.cross_functional: I work well with non-engineers when the conversation stays grounded in the actual decision or user problem. My goal is to make the technical tradeoffs clear without hiding behind jargon.
